question: What does parenteral drug administration mean in clinical practice?

options.A: Giving medications by routes outside the digestive tract
options.B: Applying medicated creams directly onto unbroken skin
options.C: Instilling liquid drops straight into the ear canal
options.D: Swallowing pills with a large glass of water

explanation: Parenteral administration bypasses the gastrointestinal tract using injections such as intravenous or intramuscular routes. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h1)

question: Why would a nurse choose the intravenous route over the oral route for a critically ill patient?

options.A: Intravenous administration requires significantly less skill and monitoring
options.B: Oral medications always cause severe local tissue necrosis
options.C: Oral medications are completely destroyed inside the bloodstream
options.D: Intravenous medications achieve a much faster onset of action

explanation: Injecting drugs directly into the bloodstream skips absorption barriers, leading to immediate systemic effects. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h1)

question: Which action demonstrates proper skin antisepsis before giving an injection?

options.A: Wiping rapidly back and forth across the entire injection site
options.B: Swabbing in a circular motion from the center outward
options.C: Applying an antiseptic swab from the outside moving inward
options.D: Scrubbing the skin vigorously with cold water and plain soap

explanation: Moving from the center outward pushes microorganisms away from the clean puncture site rather than dragging them toward it. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h2)

question: What is the primary reason nurses avoid recapping used needles with two hands?

options.A: It causes the medication remaining in the syringe to leak out
options.B: It bends the needle tip making subsequent disposal difficult
options.C: It drastically increases the risk of an accidental needlestick injury
options.D: It contaminates the sterile shaft of the needle with air

explanation: Using two hands near an exposed needle heightens the chance of piercing oneself, which risks bloodborne pathogen transmission. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h2)

question: Which needle gauge has the largest diameter bore?
explanation: Needle gauge is inversely related to diameter, meaning lower numbers indicate wider needle bores. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h3)

question: Why is a filter needle specifically required when drawing medication from a glass ampule?

options.A: To dilute concentrated medications with sterile water automatically
options.B: To prevent the active drug ingredients from evaporating into the air
options.C: To filter out large air bubbles trapped inside the liquid drug
options.D: To catch microscopic glass shards broken off during ampule opening

explanation: Snapping the neck of a glass ampule creates tiny fragments that could be injected into the patient if a filter is not used. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h3)

question: What angle of insertion is typically used for an intradermal injection?
explanation: A very shallow insertion angle keeps the needle in the dermal layer without accidentally passing into subcutaneous tissue. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h4)

question: Why is site rotation especially important for patients who receive regular subcutaneous insulin injections?

options.A: To make the daily injections completely painless over time
options.B: To prevent abnormal tissue thickening known as lipodystrophy
options.C: To keep the skin surface sterile and free from local redness
options.D: To ensure the insulin absorbs faster into the bloodstream

explanation: Using the same injection site repeatedly damages subcutaneous fat tissue, disrupting normal insulin absorption. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h4)

question: Which anatomical landmark is used when locating the ventrogluteal injection site?

options.A: Greater trochanter and anterior superior iliac spine
options.B: Acromion process and the axillary fold of the shoulder
options.C: Umbilicus and the bilateral anterior superior iliac crests
options.D: Patella and the tibial tuberosity on the lower leg

explanation: The nurse places their palm on the greater trochanter and spreads fingers toward the iliac spine to identify this safe muscle. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h5)

question: What is the primary clinical purpose of using the Z-track method for intramuscular injections?

options.A: To eliminate the need for cleaning the skin with an alcohol swab
options.B: To speed up the absorption rate of irritating watery solutions
options.C: To seal the medication inside the muscle and prevent skin staining
options.D: To push the needle deeper into bone when muscle mass is small

explanation: Displacing the skin before insertion creates a zigzag path that traps medication and prevents leakage into superficial tissues. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h5)

question: What immediate action should a nurse take if resistance is felt when flushing an intravenous catheter?

options.A: Stop flushing immediately and investigate the cause
options.B: Inject heparin rapidly to dissolve the internal clot
options.C: Push the syringe plunger harder to clear the blockage
options.D: Disconnect the line and ignore the blocked catheter

explanation: Forcing a blocked IV line can rupture the vein or dislodge a clot into the circulatory system. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h6)

question: Which local complication occurs when intravenous fluid leaks into the surrounding subcutaneous tissue?
explanation: Infiltration happens when the catheter slips out of the vein, causing infusate to enter surrounding non-vascular tissue. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h6)

question: Which laboratory values are especially critical to review before giving medications cleared through the body?

options.A: Complete blood count and blood type
options.D: Serum lipid panels and thyroid hormones

explanation: Renal and hepatic panels show how well organs process and eliminate drugs, preventing dangerous systemic accumulation. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h7)

question: How should a nurse reliably confirm a patient's identity prior to administering a parenteral drug?

options.A: Look at the chart hanging at the end of the hospital bed
options.B: Check the identification band and ask the patient to state their name
options.C: Call out the patient's surname loudly and wait for someone to nod
options.D: Ask another ward nurse if this is the correct bed occupant

explanation: Using two distinct identifiers, such as checking the ID band and asking verbal confirmation, prevents administration errors. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h7)

question: What is the very first action a nurse must take if a patient shows signs of an acute allergic reaction to an IV drug?

options.A: Document the adverse event in the nursing notes
options.B: Slow down the infusion pump rate by half
options.D: Call the attending physician for further advice

explanation: Stopping the infusion halts any further entry of the allergen into the patient's circulation. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h8)

question: Why is a patient suspected of having an air embolism placed in the left lateral Trendelenburg position?

options.A: To increase blood flow directly to the brain and prevent sudden fainting spells
options.B: To trap air bubbles in the apex of the right ventricle away from pulmonary vessels
options.C: To make it easier for the surgical team to insert a central venous catheter
options.D: To encourage rapid absorption of trapped air bubbles through the lung alveoli

explanation: This positioning keeps air away from the pulmonary outflow tract until it can be safely absorbed into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h8)

question: When should a nurse document a parenteral medication that was just administered to a patient?

options.A: Before drawing up the drug from the vial
options.B: Whenever time permits later in the day
options.D: At the very end of the working shift

explanation: Immediate documentation prevents other staff members from mistakenly administering a duplicate dose. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h9)

question: Why is a post-administration evaluation an essential responsibility for the nurse?

options.A: To confirm whether the drug achieved its desired effect and check for adverse reactions
options.B: To update the dietary department regarding changes in meal schedules
options.C: To satisfy legal hospital auditing requirements without patient interaction
options.D: To ensure the patient pays their hospital pharmacy bill on time

explanation: Evaluating the patient helps determine if the treatment worked and catches unexpected side effects early. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h9)
